proposal.description_long: An August 2016 report by The Times described a Ukrainian prosecutor’s memo about Paul Manafort’s earlier work in Crimea. The prosecutor alleged that Manafort organized anti-NATO and anti-Kyiv protests there in 2006 on behalf of Viktor Yanukovych’s Party of Regions. The Times reported that the protests led to cancellation of planned NATO exercises and quoted the memo as saying Manafort viewed autonomy as a way to bolster Yanukovych’s party among local voters. The Times said the memo set out legal options for prosecuting him but no charges were pursued after Crimea’s 2014 annexation, citing a lack of evidence. At the time of the article, Manafort was Donald Trump’s campaign chief. The story documents the existence of the allegation and the reported status of the inquiry, not a proven finding. It does not establish that Manafort caused the cancellation, aided Russia’s later annexation, or participated in Russia’s 2014 seizure of the peninsula. The 2006 alleged protests and the 2014 annexation remain distinct events.

proposal.description_long: On August 20, 2025, Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the United States would not approve wind or solar projects, describing them as harmful to farmland and asserting that states relying on them faced higher electricity costs. Bloomberg reported the post as part of Trump’s public opposition to renewable energy and noted that it followed an Agriculture Department announcement ending support programs for clean energy on productive farmland. A public statement is evidence of the president’s stated position and can be reported as such. It does not, on its own, identify the agencies or permits covered, establish a blanket legal prohibition, or show that all wind and solar approvals stopped. The supplied packet contains no project list, implementing order, agency decision, or follow-up measurement of approvals. The revised title therefore describes the statement rather than presenting its broadest possible reading as a completed administrative ban. Any account of actual implementation should identify the governing directive and distinguish projects affected from those still under review. The statement’s cost assertion is also attributed to Trump; this record does not independently assess whether renewable projects increased electricity prices.
proposal.description_medium: On August 20, 2025, Donald Trump posted that the United States would not approve wind or solar energy projects, criticizing projects he said harmed farmland and raised electricity prices. Bloomberg reported the statement and its context. The post is evidence of his stated position, while the supplied packet does not identify an implementing action or establish that all such approvals stopped.
proposal.description_short: Trump said on August 20, 2025, that his administration would not approve wind or solar projects; the post alone does not define implementation.

proposal.description_long: On January 28, 2016, Donald Trump held a nationally televised fundraiser in Iowa for veterans’ organizations while skipping a televised Republican debate. The New York Attorney General’s court filings say the event raised approximately $5.6 million and that $2.823 million of that amount was donated to the Trump Foundation, which was then expected to distribute the money to veterans’ groups. The Attorney General later alleged that the Foundation ceded control of the grants to Trump’s campaign, making the Foundation’s contribution an improper in-kind campaign contribution. That allegation and the eventual resolution belong to the later legal case; they should not be described as a finding that every fundraiser dollar was misused. In November 2019, a court separately ordered Trump to pay $2 million in damages to charities and imposed restrictions related to future charitable service. The stored January 28, 2016 date identifies the fundraiser, not that later court order. This draft aligns the title and descriptions with the dated fundraiser and clearly distinguishes the event from the judgment. The record should not combine the two dates or imply that the court order occurred in 2016.
